metadata.summary: This guideline addresses the selection and use of allergen immunotherapy for allergic rhinitis with or without conjunctivitis across age groups. Drawing on a systematic review, meta-analysis and expert input, it assesses clinical benefit, safety, treatment duration and patient- and allergen-related factors for subcutaneous and sublingual approaches. It also discusses alternative immunotherapy approaches, implementation, and gaps in the evidence, particularly concerning children and long-term outcomes.

target_population: Patients of all ages with allergic rhinitis with or without conjunctivitis

toxicities.incidence: A 3-year US survey covering over 20 million injection visits reported systemic reactions after 0.1% of injections; it reported no fatalities, although a follow-up survey by the same group reported 4. A European prospective survey of 4316 patients reported systemic reactions in 2.1% of SCIT-treated patients. Figure 2 describes a 1:2000 chance per injection of moderate-to-severe systemic allergic reactions, with a lower chance for allergoids.
recognition: Reactions can affect the skin, upper or lower airways, gastrointestinal tract, or cardiovascular system and range from mild to severe.
Over 80% of reactions in the US survey occurred within 30 minutes of injection; very few delayed reactions were severe.

In the European survey, independent risk factors were natural extracts, absence of symptomatic allergy medication, asthma, sensitization to animal dander or pollen, cluster regimens rather than rush regimens, and previous anaphylaxis.

Other reported potential risk factors include current allergic symptoms or allergen exposure, current infections, mast cell disease, a previous systemic reaction to SCIT or SLIT, uncontrolled or severe asthma, a high degree of sensitization, excessive dose escalation, beta-blocker use, poor injection technique, allergen extract overdose, failure to follow the manufacturer's dose-reduction advice when changing production batches, and high-intensity physical exercise.

management.severity: One or more severe adverse reactions
management.actions: The allergist should review the benefits and risks with the patient and decide whether SCIT should continue. Any cessation or subsequent dosing adjustment should follow the SmPC.

prevention: Give injections in a medical setting through experienced staff trained to identify and manage systemic reactions, with immediate access to resuscitation equipment and a physician trained in anaphylaxis management.
Keep patients under observation for at least 30 minutes after every injection.
Control asthma before starting AIT; uncontrolled or severe asthma is a contraindication.
Antihistamine premedication reduces local and systemic cutaneous reactions but does not prevent systemic reactions or anaphylaxis.
Studies associate modified allergen extracts with fewer adverse effects. Combining anti-IgE injections with AIT reduced systemic side-effects in the cited studies of children and adults.
toxicities.dose_modifications: After adverse effects, intercurrent illness, or delayed dosing, Box 4 describes dose reductions (usually 50%) or split doses as directed by the SCIT SmPC. After a severe reaction, cessation or changes to the next dosing schedule should follow the SmPC.

toxicities.incidence: Redness, itching, or swelling occurs after around half of injections.
recognition: An enlarged local reaction is redness and/or swelling >10 cm in diameter.
More frequent local reactions do not predict a higher individual risk of a systemic reaction.

management.actions: Cooling, topical glucocorticoids, or oral antihistamines may help.

management.severity: Enlarged local reaction >10 cm in diameter
management.actions: Use the SmPC instructions to adjust the schedule for the next injection.

prevention: H1-antihistamine premedication can reduce the frequency and severity of local adverse reactions; it does not prevent systemic reactions or anaphylaxis.
toxicities.dose_modifications: For injection-site redness and/or swelling >10 cm in diameter, adjust the next injection according to the SmPC. Box 4 describes dose reductions (usually 50%) or split doses for adverse effects, in accordance with the SmPC.

toxicities.event: Reactions associated with aluminum hydroxide-containing SCIT products
recognition: Subcutaneous granulomas have been described as foreign-body reactions, mainly following incorrect intradermal administration.
Contact allergic reactions, newly arising protein contact dermatitis, and vasculitis inflammatory reactions have also been reported.

management.severity: Reaction to an aluminum hydroxide-containing SCIT product
management.actions: A different product without aluminum hydroxide is preferred.

toxicities.dose_modifications: If subcutaneous granulomas develop, replacing the extract with one that does not contain aluminum hydroxide may be recommended.

toxicities.incidence: A review of 66 SLIT studies involving over 4000 patients and over a million doses found approximately 1 systemic reaction per 4 years of treatment and 1 severe systemic reaction per 384 treatment years. A European prospective survey reported systemic reactions in 1.1% of SLIT-treated patients. Figure 2 describes rare moderate-to-severe systemic reactions at <1:500 over 3 y.
recognition: Severe systemic reactions, sometimes including anaphylaxis, have been reported within 30 minutes of allergen administration as drops or tablets.

The reported severe cases involved departures from usual SLIT standards, including nonstandardized extracts, rush protocols, excessive allergen doses, or patients whose SCIT had previously been stopped because of severe reactions.
Uncontrolled concomitant asthma has been reported in association with severe systemic reactions.
Severe systemic reactions appear much less likely with SLIT than with SCIT, although overall adverse-reaction rates are similar.

management.severity: One or more severe adverse reactions
management.actions: The allergist should revisit the benefits and risks with the patient and decide whether SLIT should continue. Cessation or dosage changes should follow the SmPC.

prevention: Give the initial dose under supervision by staff able to manage anaphylaxis, with immediate access to resuscitation equipment and a physician trained in its management.
Observe the patient for at least 30 minutes after the first dose.
Teach patients how to identify and manage adverse reactions, especially severe ones, because most SLIT adverse events arise at home.
Explain what to do after a missed dose and when treatment should be interrupted temporarily.
toxicities.dose_modifications: After a severe reaction, interruption or dosage adjustment should follow the SmPC. Temporary interruption may be advised in the situations specified for oral injury or upper respiratory tract infection.

toxicities.event: Local mucosal reactions and abdominal pain during SLIT
toxicities.incidence: Local adverse events during SLIT are reported in 40-75%. In recent SLIT-tablet trials, these reactions led to treatment cessation in 4-8% of cases.
recognition: Transient oral pruritus or dysesthesia, oral mucosal swelling, throat irritation, or abdominal pain.
Most reactions arise early in treatment, commonly during the first 3 weeks, and are generally mild and self-limiting.

management.actions: Oral antihistamines may lessen the reaction.

prevention: Inform patients how to recognize and manage reactions and when SLIT may need to be interrupted.
toxicities.dose_modifications: Temporary cessation may be advised for 7 days after dental extraction, oral surgery, or shedding of a deciduous tooth; while an oral ulcer or open mouth wound heals; or during an upper respiratory tract infection in a patient with asthma. Product-specific SmPC advice may add other circumstances.

recognition: Local eczematous reactions at the patch application site accompanied the modest benefit observed in RCTs of epicutaneous grass pollen immunotherapy.

toxicities.event: Worsened seasonal outcomes and cutaneous Th2 inflammation with intradermal grass pollen immunotherapy
recognition: A subsequent RCT found evidence of exacerbated seasonal outcomes and Th2 inflammation in the skin; that trial did not show efficacy.

prophylaxis.recommendation: Antihistamine premedication is recommended to reduce the frequency and severity of local and systemic cutaneous reactions; it does not eliminate other systemic adverse reactions, including anaphylaxis.
Asthma should be controlled before AIT begins because insufficient control increases risk with both SCIT and SLIT. Uncontrolled or severe asthma is a contraindication.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients with asthma being considered for AIT

prophylaxis.recommendation: Administer SCIT through competent personnel with immediate resuscitation equipment and a physician trained in anaphylaxis management, and keep the patient under observation after each injection.
prophylaxis.duration: At least 30 minutes after each injection

prophylaxis.recommendation: Administer the first SLIT dose under competent supervision with access to resuscitation equipment and a physician trained in anaphylaxis management, then observe the patient.
prophylaxis.duration: At least 30 minutes after the initial dose

prophylaxis.recommendation: Patients receiving SLIT should be taught to identify and manage adverse reactions, particularly severe reactions, and advised about missed doses and circumstances requiring temporary interruption.

Temporary cessation may be advised after dental extraction, oral surgery, or shedding of a deciduous tooth; while an oral ulcer or open wound heals; or during an upper respiratory tract infection in a patient with asthma. Additional product-specific advice may appear in the SmPC.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients receiving SLIT who experience the specified circumstances
prophylaxis.duration: For 7 days following dental extraction, oral surgery, or shedding of a deciduous tooth; while an oral ulcer or open mouth wound heals; or during an upper respiratory tract infection in patients with asthma

infection_management.management: For patients with asthma receiving SLIT, temporary treatment cessation during an upper respiratory tract infection may be advised.

conditions.name: Allergic rhinoconjunctivitis
synonyms: allergic rhinitis with or without conjunctivitis
conditions.description: Allergic disease involving the nose and, when present, the eyes. It produces chronic inflammation of the nasal mucosa and conjunctiva that is predominantly eosinophilic. The guideline uses AR to include allergic rhinitis whether or not conjunctivitis is present.
conditions.epidemiology: Allergic rhinitis, with or without conjunctivitis, affects around a fifth of the general population. Most patients with AR are polysensitized.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Typical nasal symptoms are itching, sneezing, watery discharge and congestion; the eyes may water, redden or itch. Symptoms occur with exposure to a relevant aeroallergen and may also be affected by smoke, dust, viral infections, strong odors or cold air. Sinusitis symptoms, hearing problems and asthma may accompany AR. Other forms of rhinitis can coexist and alter the presentation.

subtypes.name: perennial allergic rhinitis
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Symptoms occur on a perennial rather than seasonal pattern.

subtypes.name: grass pollen-driven AR
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Grass pollen exposure is identified as driving the allergic symptoms.

subtypes.name: perennial HDM AR
subtypes.distinguishing_features: HDM is identified as the relevant allergen in perennial disease.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Establish the symptom pattern, its relationship to aeroallergen exposure and possible alternative or coexisting forms of rhinitis.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During assessment of suspected AR and before selecting an allergen for AIT.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Typical symptoms linked to exposure support AR; exposure-related symptoms together with sensitization to the relevant allergen confirm the diagnosis.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify IgE sensitization to allergens implicated by the history.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During diagnostic assessment and selection of clinically relevant allergens for AIT.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A positive result supports AR when the tested allergen is relevant to the exposure and symptom history.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify sensitization to allergens implicated by the history.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During diagnostic assessment and selection of clinically relevant allergens for AIT.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Detection supports AR when the allergen matches the exposure and symptom history.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Help identify which aeroallergen is driving symptoms in a polysensitized patient.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: May be considered when SPT or specific IgE results do not clearly identify the relevant allergen.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Its role in allergen selection remains uncertain because definitive trials are awaited.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess whether sensitization is clinically relevant in the affected organ.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: May be considered before AIT when the symptom-driving allergen is unclear, particularly in polysensitized patients.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A response can support clinical relevance, but definitive evidence for this approach is awaited.

staging.additional_rules: Symptoms may be described as seasonal or perennial, intermittent or persistent, and mild, moderate or severe according to their effect on quality of life.

prognostic_tools.name: Allergic Rhinitis and its Impact on Asthma (ARIA)
components: Interference with usual daily activities or sleep

risk_groups.criteria: Moderate-to-severe symptoms that interfere with usual daily activities or sleep.

prognostic_tools.interpretation: The guideline cites these categories to describe disease severity when considering AIT; it does not provide a prognostic estimate.

follow_up.schedule: For patients receiving SLIT, follow-up every 3 mo can be recommended to improve adherence. During AIT, reassess adherence, benefit and adverse effects regularly; reassess treatment if the patient and physician find no benefit after 1 y.
long_term_effects: After an adequate course of AIT, clinical benefit may persist following treatment cessation.
Long-term efficacy is assessed at least 1 y after the AIT course ends.
follow_up.survivorship_notes: At least 3 y of AIT is recommended when the aim is lasting efficacy after treatment stops; selected patients may require longer treatment.

therapies_index.name: AIT
therapies_index.mechanism: Repeated exposure to the relevant allergen is intended to alter the immune response, lessen allergic symptoms and medication requirements, and potentially modify the course of disease.
approved_indications: Allergic rhinitis, with or without conjunctivitis, when symptoms are linked to a clinically relevant allergen and IgE sensitization is demonstrated.
Moderate-to-severe AR that disrupts daily activities or sleep despite appropriate pharmacotherapy and/or avoidance measures.
Less severe AR may also warrant consideration when a patient seeks lasting benefit or the potential to prevent asthma with grass pollen AIT.
therapies_index.administration: The relevant allergen is given repeatedly by the subcutaneous or sublingual route. A minimum of 3 years is recommended when long-term efficacy after stopping treatment is the goal.
monitoring: Assess clinical benefit, adverse effects and adherence regularly.
Reconsider benefits and risks with the patient after 1 or more severe adverse reactions; follow the SmPC when altering or stopping treatment.

therapies_index.name: SCIT
approved_indications: Short-term treatment of seasonal or perennial AR that remains suboptimally controlled despite pharmacotherapy.
Long-term treatment benefit in grass pollen-driven AR after an adequate course.
therapies_index.administration: Allergen is administered by subcutaneous injection in a medical setting by trained staff. Treatment may be continuous, preseasonal or pre-/coseasonal, as applicable; maintenance injections are usually monthly.
key_toxicities: Systemic allergic reactions that can involve the skin, airways, gastrointestinal tract or cardiovascular system
monitoring: Observe the patient in the clinic for at least 30 minutes after each injection.
Ensure immediate access to resuscitation equipment and a physician trained to manage anaphylaxis.
Reassess benefits and risks after 1 or more severe adverse reactions.
Consult the SmPC for changes to the next dose after an enlarged local reaction or other circumstances requiring dose adjustment.

therapies_index.name: continuous SCIT
approved_indications: Short-term benefit in seasonal AR.
Short-term benefit in perennial AR due to HDM.
therapies_index.administration: Subcutaneous injections are given throughout the year.
monitoring: Observe in the clinic for at least 30 minutes after each injection.

therapies_index.name: pre- and pre-/coseasonal SCIT
approved_indications: Short-term benefit in seasonal AR.
therapies_index.administration: Subcutaneous treatment is given before the pollen season or before and during that season.
monitoring: Observe in the clinic for at least 30 minutes after each injection.

therapies_index.name: continuous grass pollen SCIT
approved_indications: Short- and long-term benefit in seasonal AR driven by grass pollen.
therapies_index.administration: Grass pollen allergen is administered as year-round subcutaneous injections; grass pollen SCIT given for 3-4 years produced lasting efficacy in a cited study.
monitoring: Observe in the clinic for at least 30 minutes after each injection.

therapies_index.name: modified (allergoids) and unmodified allergen extracts
approved_indications: Short-term treatment of AR with pollen or HDM SCIT extracts.
therapies_index.administration: Used for subcutaneous immunotherapy; preparations may be aqueous or depot formulations adsorbed on aluminum hydroxide or tyrosine.
key_toxicities: Local and systemic allergic reactions associated with SCIT
monitoring: Assess efficacy evidence for the individual product before starting treatment.
Follow the product-specific SmPC and observe patients for at least 30 minutes after injections.

therapies_index.name: aluminum hydroxide containing SCIT products
therapies_index.administration: Administered by subcutaneous injection.
key_toxicities: Foreign-body granulomas, chiefly described after incorrect intradermal administration
monitoring: If these reactions arise, reassess treatment; an aluminum hydroxide-free product is preferred.

therapies_index.name: SLIT
approved_indications: Short-term treatment of seasonal AR.
Short-term treatment of perennial AR with effective tablet preparations.

special_populations.population: Polysensitized patients who are clinically monoallergic
special_populations.considerations: Although sensitization to multiple allergens is present, only 1 allergen drives symptoms. Clinical history may identify it; component-resolved diagnostics or nasal or conjunctival provocation testing may help when the relevant allergen remains unclear.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: AIT is recommended for the specific allergen responsible for AR symptoms (Grade A).

special_populations.population: Polysensitized patients who are poly-allergic to homologous allergens
special_populations.considerations: Symptoms arise during exposure to multiple biologically related allergens. The preparation should cover the major relevant allergens from that biological family.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: A single allergen preparation or a mixture of homologous allergens can be recommended (Grade B).

special_populations.population: Patients who are poly-allergic to nonhomologous allergens
special_populations.considerations: When several unrelated allergens drive symptoms, immunotherapy may be less effective. The choice of allergens requires a balance between efficacy and safety.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: AIT may be recommended for the allergen causing most symptoms, or separate preparations may be used for the 2 clinically most important allergens. If 2 are selected, administer doses 30-60 minutes apart at separate locations (Grade C).

special_populations.considerations: Controlled mild-to-moderate asthma does not appear to compromise AIT safety or reduce its efficacy for AR. Evidence concerning partially controlled asthma requires confirmation. Uncontrolled or severe asthma is an absolute contraindication to AIT.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Control asthma before starting AIT. With partially controlled asthma, use AIT only cautiously when the potential benefit outweighs the risk for the individual patient.

special_populations.considerations: AIT should be considered when AR is accompanied by IgE sensitization to clinically relevant allergens. Evidence for efficacy is limited in children younger than 5 years of age, and repeated SCIT injections may be stressful for preschool children. More evidence is available for school-age children and adolescents, although important gaps remain.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: For children aged 2-5 y of age, decide whether to start AIT case by case with the child and family, considering disease severity, the exposure–symptom pattern and sensitization tests, quality-of-life effects, and likely acceptance and adherence (Grade D). For seasonal AR, continuous or pre- and pre-/coseasonal SCIT can be recommended (Grade B), and pre-/coseasonal or continuous SLIT is recommended (Grade A). Continuous SCIT is recommended for perennial AR (Grade C). For perennial allergic rhinitis, aqueous SLIT solutions lack consistent supporting data, whereas SLIT tablets have shown short-term effectiveness in mixed adult/adolescent studies (grade A).

special_populations.considerations: Other forms of rhinitis may resemble AR, making a detailed allergy history especially important. Evidence specifically involving adults >65 years is sparse. Comorbidities and beta-blocker treatment may affect the risks of AIT or the treatment of anaphylaxis.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: AIT can be recommended for otherwise healthy elderly patients whose AR remains inadequately controlled with pharmacotherapy (Grade A for SLIT, B for SCIT).

special_populations.considerations: Available studies suggest no greater risk of prematurity, fetal abnormality, or other adverse pregnancy outcomes among women receiving AIT during pregnancy, but systemic reactions and their treatment could harm the mother and/or baby. Benefits and potential risks should be discussed with the patient.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Do not initiate AIT during pregnancy (Grade D). Previously well-tolerated AIT may be continued during pregnancy or breastfeeding, in agreement with the patient’s GP and obstetrician (Grade C); maintenance immunotherapy may continue at the achieved dose.

special_populations.population: Patients with other contraindications or conditions requiring caution
special_populations.considerations: Active, systemic autoimmune disorders unresponsive to treatment and active malignant neoplasia are considered contraindications to AIT. Beta-blocker therapy, severe cardiovascular disease, systemic autoimmune disorders in remission or confined to an organ, severe psychiatric disorders, poor adherence, primary or secondary immunodeficiencies, and a history of serious systemic reactions to AIT call for an individual assessment of benefits and risks.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: For conditions requiring caution, use AIT only when the expected benefit outweighs the potential risk. Review the SmPC for contraindications specific to the preparation.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with allergic rhinitis, with or without conjunctivitis.
decision_rules: Use symptom control and reduction of inflammation as the initial management goals.
Consider allergen avoidance where feasible; effective avoidance is often difficult.
If symptoms remain troublesome despite appropriate regular treatment and avoidance measures, assess eligibility for AIT.

recommended_regimens.name: pharmacotherapy
recommended_regimens.summary: Symptom-directed options described include oral or topical antihistamines, intranasal corticosteroids, topical cromoglycate and leukotriene receptor antagonists. These treatments do not change the natural history of AR and may cause side-effects.

response_assessment.method: Assess symptom control and effects on usual daily activities and sleep.
response_assessment.interpretation: Persistent impairment despite appropriate treatment supports consideration of AIT.

supportive_care: Recommend allergen avoidance where possible.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guide does not present symptom-directed pharmacotherapy as disease-modifying treatment.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients of any age with symptoms strongly suggestive of AR, with or without conjunctivitis, and moderate-to-severe symptoms that disrupt daily activities or sleep despite regular, appropriate pharmacotherapy and/or avoidance measures.
treatment_pathways.biomarker_condition: IgE sensitization to 1 or more clinically relevant allergens, shown by positive SPT and/or serum-specific IgE.
decision_rules: Match the allergen used for AIT to the exposure that drives the patient's symptoms.
Before prescribing a particular preparation, evaluate its own clinical evidence of efficacy and check its SmPC for licensed indications and contraindications.
Use standardized AIT products with documented efficacy when available; results for one product should not be assumed to apply to another.
Discuss SCIT and SLIT in light of documented product efficacy, safety, practical requirements, cost and patient preference. The evidence does not establish which route is more effective.
Do not initiate AIT in the presence of uncontrolled or severe asthma, active systemic autoimmune disease unresponsive to treatment, active malignant neoplasia, or pregnancy.

recommended_regimens.name: AIT
recommended_regimens.summary: Consider allergen-directed immunotherapy when the stated symptom, sensitization and inadequate-control criteria are all met. Either SCIT or SLIT may be used with an appropriately supported product.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: The guideline's meta-analysis associated both SCIT and SLIT with reduced symptoms and medication use, but found insufficient data to determine which is more effective.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: A minimum of 3 years is recommended when lasting benefit after treatment cessation is the goal.

response_assessment.interpretation: Selected patients may warrant a longer course.

Explain expected benefits, adverse effects and the need for regular dosing and completion of treatment.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Polysensitized patients who are clinically poly-allergic to allergens from nonrelated biological families.
treatment_pathways.biomarker_condition: Clinically relevant sensitization to nonhomologous allergens.
decision_rules: Prioritize the allergen causing most AR symptoms or treat the 2 clinically most important allergens separately.
If 2 preparations are used, administer doses 30-60 minutes apart at separate sites rather than combining nonrelated allergens.

recommended_regimens.name: AIT directed at the allergen responsible for most symptoms

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients for whom an uncommon, clinically relevant allergen creates a need for AIT despite sparse or absent robust RCT evidence.
treatment_pathways.biomarker_condition: Sensitization to the allergen judged responsible for symptoms.

response_assessment.method: Assess the effect on the patient's clinical symptoms.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guideline calls for controlled efficacy and safety studies where feasible and notes that some orphan allergens must be regulated as named-patient products.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with AR for whom the listed additional immunotherapy approaches are clinically relevant.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Children aged 2-5 y with AR for whom AIT is being considered.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Otherwise healthy elderly patients with AR whose symptoms remain inadequately controlled by pharmacotherapy; the guideline defines elderly here as >65 years.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients who become pregnant after starting an AIT course that they previously tolerated well, or who are breastfeeding after such treatment.

recommended_regimens.name: AIT

document_sections.heading: Abstract
document_sections.content: Allergic rhinoconjunctivitis (AR) affects the nose and eyes and occurs in about a fifth of the general population. Allergen avoidance and medication can control symptoms, but many patients remain symptomatic, experience impaired quality of life, or have medication-related adverse effects. Allergen immunotherapy (AIT), delivered as subcutaneous immunotherapy (SCIT) or sublingual immunotherapy (SLIT), addresses the underlying disease process and may modify its course. This EAACI guideline draws on a systematic review, meta-analysis, and stakeholder input and was developed using the AGREE II approach. Evidence broadly supports AIT for AR, but efficacy should be assessed for each product. SCIT and SLIT are generally recommended for short-term benefit in seasonal and perennial AR. Evidence for benefit after treatment is strongest for grass AIT, especially grass tablets. At least 3 years of treatment is recommended to obtain long-term efficacy. Important evidence gaps remain, particularly for long-term outcomes and children.

document_sections.heading: 1 | INTRODUCTION
document_sections.content: AR causes chronic inflammation, predominantly eosinophilic, in the nasal mucosa and conjunctiva. Allergic rhinitis, whether or not accompanied by conjunctivitis, affects around a fifth of the general population and is associated with reduced productivity and poorer school performance. Typical nasal symptoms are itching, sneezing, watery discharge, and obstruction; watery, red, or itchy eyes commonly accompany them. Symptoms may be seasonal or perennial, intermittent or persistent, and mild, moderate, or severe according to their effect on quality of life. They occur with the causative allergen and can also respond to smoke, dust, viral infections, strong odors, or cold air. Symptoms during exposure to 1 or more aeroallergens, together with relevant allergen-specific IgE sensitization, establish the diagnosis. Other forms of rhinitis can coexist, and sinusitis symptoms, hearing difficulties, or asthma can also occur. The differential diagnosis includes infectious rhinitis and structural, neurogenic, hormonal, drug-induced, irritant, and other nonallergic, noninfectious causes. Local allergic rhinitis can involve sensitization detectable only in the nose. Multiple triggers may influence an individual's presentation and treatment response. AIT is indicated for allergic rhinitis or rhinoconjunctivitis, not other forms of rhinitis; rhinosinusitis is outside this guideline's scope. Management seeks symptom control and reduced inflammation. Allergen avoidance can be recommended where feasible, although effective avoidance is often impractical. Oral or topical antihistamines, intranasal corticosteroids, topical cromoglycate, and leukotriene receptor antagonists are medication options, but do not change the natural history of AR and may cause adverse effects. Symptoms impair quality of life in a significant number of patients despite medication. SCIT or SLIT using the responsible allergen may reduce symptoms through desensitization and provide benefits persisting for years after treatment stops. AIT involves repeated allergen administration to alter the immune response, reduce symptoms and medication needs, and potentially prevent new allergies and asthma. Short-term efficacy refers to benefit during treatment; long-term efficacy refers to benefit for at least 1 y after treatment ends. Rhinitis entails inflammation with at least 2 of rhinorrhea, obstruction, sneezing, or itching. Sensitization is detectable allergen-specific IgE on skin prick test (SPT) and/or serum testing. SCIT uses subcutaneous injections; SLIT uses drops or rapidly dissolving tablets beneath the tongue. This guideline addresses AIT for allergic rhinitis with or without conjunctivitis at all ages. Its principal audience is clinical allergists, although it also addresses other healthcare professionals in primary, secondary, and tertiary care. A formal systematic review and meta-analysis informed its development.

document_sections.heading: 2 | METHODOLOGY
document_sections.content: The guideline used the AGREE II approach to involve relevant stakeholders, search and appraise evidence, formulate recommendations systematically, and minimize bias. Work began in April 2015 with in-person discussions about methods and clinical priorities, followed by further meetings and web conferences involving professional and lay participants.

document_sections.heading: 2.1 | Clarifying the scope and purpose of the guidelines
document_sections.content: The guideline provides statements to help clinicians use AIT optimally for AR and identifies research gaps.

document_sections.heading: 2.2 | Ensuring appropriate stakeholder involvement
document_sections.content: The EAACI task force included participants from 18 countries and brought together allergy and other clinical specialties, pharmacists, nurses, methodologists, and patient representatives. Methodologists led the underlying systematic review, while clinical academics led the development of care recommendations. Product manufacturers could comment during final peer review and public consultation; the task force considered their feedback and revised the guideline where appropriate.

document_sections.heading: 2.3 | Systematic reviews of the evidence
document_sections.content: After refining its clinical questions, the task force focused on the effectiveness, cost-effectiveness, and safety of AIT in AR. Independent methodologists conducted the published systematic review; effectiveness analyses included only double-blind RCTs. The task force monitored publications appearing after the October 31, 2015 review cutoff and considered relevant studies, while reserving their formal assessment for the systematic review preceding the next guideline update.

document_sections.heading: 2.4 | Formulating recommendations
document_sections.content: Key systematic-review findings were assessed for strength and consistency, and random-effects meta-analyses accounted for heterogeneity. Recommendations link their wording to evidence strength: strong recommendations use 'is recommended', moderate recommendations use 'can be recommended', weak recommendations allow use in specific circumstances, and negative recommendations state that use cannot be recommended. Level I covers systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and randomized controlled trials; Level II, nonrandomized studies with 2 groups; Level III, nonrandomized studies with 1 group; Level IV, descriptive outcome studies; and Level V, case reports or expert opinion. Grade A corresponds to consistent level I studies; Grade B to consistent level II or III studies or extrapolation from level I; Grade C to level IV studies or extrapolation from level II or III; and Grade D to level V evidence or troubling inconsistency or inconclusiveness at any level. Strong, Moderate, and Weak also reflect low, moderate, and high risk of bias, respectively. Where the principal review did not cover a question, the task force considered other systematic reviews, their RCTs, other known RCTs, and finally task-force consensus. Recommendations apply across ages unless stated otherwise. Where pediatric evidence was insufficient but adult findings were considered biologically applicable, the pediatric recommendation was downgraded by at least 1 level. The task force also assessed resources, implementation barriers and facilitators, implementation approaches, and potential audit criteria.

document_sections.heading: 2.5 | Peer review and public comment
document_sections.content: Invited external experts reviewed the draft. A 3-week public consultation on the EAACI website in May 2017 provided further stakeholder feedback. The task force considered the comments and made revisions where appropriate.

document_sections.heading: 2.6 | Identification of evidence gaps
document_sections.content: Guideline development identified research gaps and assigned them priorities, presented in Table 10.

document_sections.heading: 2.8 | Updating the guidelines
document_sections.content: EAACI planned an update in 2022, or earlier if important advances warranted one.

document_sections.heading: 3 | GENERAL CONSIDERATIONS BEFORE INITIATING AIT FOR AR
document_sections.content: Before AIT begins, clinicians should establish that clinically relevant allergic sensitization explains the patient's symptoms, assess whether symptoms warrant treatment, select a preparation supported by efficacy evidence, and consider contraindications.

document_sections.heading: 3.1 | General considerations
document_sections.content: AIT is indicated only when symptoms strongly suggest AR, with or without conjunctivitis, and aeroallergen exposure produces symptoms alongside a positive SPT or serum-specific IgE result for a relevant allergen. Asthma frequently coexists. Identifying the allergen driving symptoms guides selection of the AIT preparation. In polysensitized patients, SPT and serum results may not identify the principal cause clearly. Component-resolved diagnostics or nasal or conjunctival provocation testing may help establish clinical relevance, but definitive evidence for these approaches is awaited. AIT is indicated for moderate-to-severe symptoms that disturb daily activities or sleep despite avoidance measures and pharmacotherapy, including the ARIA moderate-to-severe intermittent or persistent categories. It may also be considered for less severe AR when patients seek lasting rhinitis benefit and possible asthma prevention. The general indications, supporting references, and contextual considerations appear in Table 1. Standardized products supported by clinical efficacy documentation should be used when available, because effectiveness varies substantially between products and formulations. Product-specific efficacy evidence and licensed indications in the SmPC should be checked. Evidence cited in this section indicates that appropriate AIT may reduce symptoms after treatment and that grass pollen AIT may prevent asthma in the short term, up to 2 y post-AIT.

document_sections.heading: 3.2 | Absolute and relative contraindications
document_sections.content: Even when AIT otherwise suits a patient, its potential risks must be weighed against expected benefit, and the individual preparation's SmPC should be checked. Table 2 distinguishes contraindications from circumstances requiring caution. Uncontrolled or severe asthma, active systemic autoimmune disease unresponsive to treatment, active malignancy, and starting AIT during pregnancy are contraindications. The task force based several of these judgments on weak risk evidence from adverse-event case reports or series. AIT already tolerated before pregnancy may continue. Partially controlled asthma warrants caution pending confirmatory safety evidence. Beta-blocker treatment, locally or systemically, and serious cardiovascular disease may complicate tolerance or management of anaphylaxis. Autoimmune disease in remission or limited to an organ, severe psychiatric disease, poor adherence, primary or secondary immunodeficiency, and previous serious systemic reactions to AIT require individualized discussion of benefits and risks.

document_sections.heading: 4 | AIT FOR AR: EVIDENCE-BASED, CLINICAL RECOMMENDATIONS
document_sections.content: The underpinning meta-analysis generally found that SCIT and SLIT reduced AR symptoms and medication use, but did not provide enough evidence to establish which route is more effective. Moderate to substantial heterogeneity for some outcomes reflected differences in study design and outcomes, patient populations, and products. An individual product-based efficacy assessment is strongly recommended before treatment; some products lack adequate evidence for clinical use. Only standardized products with documented efficacy should generally be prescribed, apart from the qualified consideration of orphan allergens. Local regulation and availability vary across Europe. SCIT is generally recommended for children and adults with moderate-to-severe AR that remains inadequately controlled with medication. Evidence for short-term continuous SCIT is stronger for seasonal disease, Grade A in adults, than perennial disease, Grade B in adults; perennial studies are fewer and more heterogeneous. Preseasonal or pre-/coseasonal SCIT is recommended for seasonal AR, Grade A in adults. Pre-/coseasonal treatment is shorter, although 1 direct trial suggested greater efficacy with continuous treatment. SCIT can use an aqueous preparation or a depot preparation adsorbed on aluminum hydroxide or tyrosine. Modified and unmodified allergen extracts are recommended for short-term benefit, Grade A in adults. The meta-analysis reported symptom-score results against placebo for unmodified extracts as SMD [95% CI] 0.65 [ 0.93, 0.36] and for allergoids/polymerized extracts as 0.60 [ 0.89, 0.31], with supportive medication-use and combined-score findings; no placebo-controlled randomized head-to-head comparison established differences in efficacy or adverse events. SLIT can generally be recommended for seasonal AR in adults and children with moderate-to-severe disease inadequately controlled by medication. Continuous or pre-/coseasonal SLIT is recommended, starting at least 2 months and ideally 4 months before pollen season, Grade A in adults. Daily SLIT can be administered as a rapidly dissolving tablet or drops held beneath the tongue for at least 1 minute before swallowing, subject to product-specific SmPC instructions. For seasonal AR, tablets and drops are recommended on short-term evidence, with adult grades A and B, respectively. Convincing efficacy evidence for perennial AR is confined to SLIT tablets, Grade A. Grass pollen SLIT tablets for at least 3 years are recommended for short-term treatment of grass pollen-driven AR in adults, Grade A; HDM SLIT tablets for at least 1 year are recommended for short-term treatment of perennial HDM AR in adults, Grade A. Higher individual or cumulative doses may improve efficacy but may also increase adverse effects, so dosing decisions must balance both. Table 3 sets out route, schedule, formulation, age-specific evidence and grades, and short- or long-term benefit. Its recommendations include continuous grass pollen SCIT and continuous grass pollen SLIT tablets or solution for longer-term benefit; they do not recommend aqueous SLIT solutions for short-term treatment of perennial AR. The table defines long-term benefit as lasting at least 1 y after AIT cessation and notes that not every preparation is licensed for children or adolescents.

document_sections.heading: 4.1 | Other approaches of AIT for AR
document_sections.content: Other approaches seek shorter, more convenient courses without sacrificing efficacy and while reducing systemic adverse effects. Combining the TLR-4 agonist monophosphoryl lipid A with a pollen allergoid is recommended for AR in Table 4; grass-allergoid studies found efficacy, although a phase 3 study found only modest efficacy. The adult recommendation is Grade A and the pediatric recommendation Grade B. There is no head-to-head comparison with conventional preparations. A ragweed trial and a tree-pollen trial also reported efficacy. A TLR-9 agonist linked to Amb a 1 was effective in a phase 2 study, but a later phase 3 study did not reproduce that finding. Studies in children and adults found that adding anti-IgE injections to conventional or rush AIT with unmodified extracts markedly reduced systemic adverse effects; the combination is recommended, Grade A. Cost and uncertainty about stopping anti-IgE after AIT maintenance are concerns. Recombinant AIT permits more precise product standardization and might allow tailoring to sensitization profiles or lower the risk of new sensitization, although the latter remains hypothetical. Trials reported efficacy without safety concerns for subcutaneous recombinant birch Bet v 1 and a five-recombinant grass allergen mixture, Grade A for adults and Grade B for children; commercially available products were lacking. A recombinant B-cell epitope-based grass vaccine combined with a hepatitis B Pre-S carrier showed efficacy in a phase 2 trial. Intradermal short T-cell epitope mixtures for cat allergy appeared promising in phase 2 environmental-chamber studies, but a subsequent phase 3 study reportedly did not demonstrate efficacy. Studies of other peptides were ongoing. Epicutaneous grass pollen immunotherapy produced modest benefit in RCTs but caused eczema-like reactions at the application site. Intradermal grass pollen treatment suppressed allergen-induced delayed skin responses, yet a later RCT found no efficacy and suggested worsened seasonal outcomes and skin Th2 inflammation. Intralymphatic treatment with grass pollen or modified cat extract was effective in some studies but not others.

document_sections.heading: 5 | ALLERGEN FACTORS THAT MAY AFFECT THE EFFICACY OF AIT FOR AR
document_sections.content: Allergen identity, extract standardization, formulation, and decisions about mixing allergens affect the evidence applicable to an AIT product. Tables and recommendations in this part distinguish supported preparations from combinations or orphan products with limited evidence.

document_sections.heading: 5.1 | Standardization of allergen extracts
document_sections.content: Characterized, stable, standardized preparations are available for many common allergens, consistent with EMA recommendations. Molds and some other allergens pose difficulties because of complexity, variability, and instability. Lack of standardization can impede diagnosis of candidates and diminish AIT effectiveness; batch-to-batch variation may increase adverse-effect risk. Further purification and characterization may improve future extracts. Standardized allergen products should be used wherever possible.

document_sections.heading: 5.2 | Formulation of SLIT preparations
document_sections.content: Formulation matters when choosing AIT. 3 large studies found HDM SLIT tablets effective, whereas 3 studies of HDM SLIT drops were negative and another found efficacy in the first but not the second year. Differences in allergen content, administered volume, sample size, and statistical power could explain differences between tablet and drop studies. AIT products with documented clinical efficacy should be used when available.

document_sections.heading: 5.3 | Allergen mixtures
document_sections.content: Grass-pollen and tree-pollen mixtures are commonly used and effective. Evidence for mixing allergens that are not taxonomically related in 1 product is very limited. One SCIT study found a depigmented-polymerized grass/birch extract superior to placebo, and a small pediatric study found efficacy with combined grass pollen and HDM SLIT. In another study, Phleum pratense SLIT drops worked better alone than at an equivalent dose within a 9-pollen mixture. Mixing may dilute allergens, permit enzyme-related degradation, and make efficacy difficult to demonstrate across numerous combinations. EMA recommends mixing only homologous allergens and never including allergens with enzymatic activity, such as HDM, in a mixture. Until additional efficacy evidence is available, the guideline recommends mixing only homologous allergens, Grade A; alternatively, extracts should be administered separately. Table 5 presents allergen-selection recommendations and evidence by age. It advises against mixtures from unrelated biological families, while recognizing an effective, individually studied grass/tree product as an exception.

document_sections.heading: 5.4 | Specific allergens
document_sections.content: The cited meta-analysis supported short-term effectiveness in allergen-specific subgroup analyses for HDM, grass, tree, and weed pollens. It printed the HDM symptom-score result as SMD 0.73; 95% CI 1.37, 0.10; grass pollen as 0.45; 0.54, 0.36; tree pollen as 0.57; 0.92, 0.21; and weed pollen as 0.68; 1.06, 0.30. Substantial heterogeneity applied across allergens, particularly molds, reported as 0.56; 2.29, 1.18. The presentation of these figures does not clearly retain their signs, so their direction should not be inferred from the printed values alone. Efficacy evidence should be assessed for each product before use. For orphan allergens, robust RCT evidence may be scarce or absent. If there is a clinical need, clinicians should weigh available efficacy and safety evidence against individual circumstances and assess symptoms early after starting treatment to decide whether to continue. Controlled trials of orphan products are encouraged, although some will remain uneconomic to study and require named-patient regulation.

document_sections.heading: 6 | PATIENT FACTORS THAT MAY IMPACT ON THE EFFICACY OF AIT FOR AR
document_sections.content: AIT works only when directed at allergens actually driving symptoms. A careful history and sensitization assessment are therefore essential to patient selection. Not everyone benefits from AIT, and better methods for identifying likely responders would be useful.

document_sections.heading: 6.1 | Polysensitized patients
document_sections.content: Most patients with AR are polysensitized. Clinicians should distinguish patients with sensitization to several allergens but symptoms caused by only 1 from patients whose symptoms follow overlapping exposure to several allergens. Single-allergen AIT works in the first situation; studies in the second have found it ineffective or less effective. History may establish the distinction, while component-resolved diagnostics or nasal or conjunctival challenge may help when performed by an experienced clinician. Patients who are polysensitized but clinically monoallergic are recommended to receive AIT for the symptom-driving allergen, Grade A. For poly-allergy to homologous allergens, a single preparation or a mixture of 2 homologous allergens is recommended, Grade B. For nonhomologous poly-allergy, separate preparations targeting 1 or 2 of the most clinically important allergens might be recommended, Grade C; where 2 are given, doses should be separated by 30-60 minutes and administered at different sites. This choice balances efficacy against safety, both of which appear dose-dependent. Additional studies are needed.

document_sections.heading: 6.2 | Co-existing asthma
document_sections.content: Asthma commonly coexists in AR AIT studies. Coexisting asthma does not reduce AIT efficacy for AR and may itself improve. Controlled mild-to-moderate asthma does not appear to raise a safety concern, Grade A, and controlled asthma is not a contraindication. 1 large SLIT asthma trial safely included some participants whose asthma was not well controlled according to ACQ-6, but confirmatory evidence is awaited. Asthma should be controlled before AIT starts. Uncontrolled or severe asthma is an absolute contraindication.

document_sections.heading: 6.3 | Specific pediatric issues
document_sections.content: As in adults, AIT should be considered for children with AR and IgE sensitization to clinically relevant allergens, Grade A. Evidence is limited below 5 years of age, although some studies found SCIT and SLIT effective and safe in preschool children; several adequately powered SLIT tablet trials enrolled children from 5 years onward. Repeated SCIT injections may distress preschool children. Starting AIT in a young child should be decided individually with the family, Grade D, taking account of disease severity, a clear exposure–symptom relationship supported by sensitization tests, impaired quality of life, and likely acceptance and adherence. Table 6 describes a Grade D consideration of benefits and risks for children aged 2-5 y. Evidence for school-age children and adolescents is greater but still incomplete: many SCIT trials are older, small, or do not report pediatric-only analyses. Continuous and pre- or pre-/coseasonal SCIT can be recommended for seasonal AR, Grade B; continuous SCIT is recommended for perennial AR with the weaker Grade C because pediatric-only evidence is lacking. Pediatric-only placebo-controlled data for allergoids are absent. 1 controlled preseasonal grass-pollen study reported lasting benefit, and 2 additional open RCTs suggested long-term benefit from grass-pollen SCIT. More recent pediatric studies support SLIT. Pre-/coseasonal and continuous SLIT are recommended for seasonal AR, Grade A, as are tablet and aqueous preparations, Grade A. A recently published trial supports long-term efficacy of a grass-pollen tablet and reduced asthma symptoms, Grade A. Evidence is weaker for perennial disease: aqueous SLIT lacks consistent supporting data, while tablet efficacy over the short term has been demonstrated in mixed adult/adolescent studies, grade A.

document_sections.heading: 6.4 | Elderly
document_sections.content: Older adults with rhinitis need a particularly careful allergy history because other rhinitis types can resemble AR. Few AIT studies specifically assess people >65 years, an age commonly excluded from trials. 2 studies found grass-pollen and HDM SLIT effective and safe, with clinical responses comparable to those in younger study populations. Comorbid hypertension, coronary or cerebrovascular disease, malignancy, and arrhythmias are relevant to treatment decisions. Beta-blockers can impair treatment of anaphylaxis with adrenaline (epinephrine). AIT can be recommended for otherwise healthy older patients whose AR remains inadequately controlled with medication, Grade A for SLIT and B for SCIT.

document_sections.heading: 6.5 | Pregnancy
document_sections.content: 1 prospective study and several retrospective studies suggest that AIT during pregnancy does not increase prematurity, fetal abnormalities, or other adverse pregnancy outcomes. Case-report observations concerning anaphylaxis in pregnancy and breastfeeding are generally reassuring, but systemic reactions and their treatment could harm the mother or baby. Benefits and risks should be discussed with the patient. Starting AIT during pregnancy is not recommended, Grade D. If treatment was started earlier and tolerated well, it may continue during pregnancy or breastfeeding after agreement with the patient's GP and obstetrician, Grade C.

document_sections.heading: 6.6 | Adherence
document_sections.content: Definitions and measured rates of AIT adherence vary greatly across trials and routine-care studies. Reported adherence ranged from 18% to over 90%; rates were generally higher in trials, with overlapping SCIT and SLIT ranges. Adverse effects, inconvenience, perceived lack of efficacy, and forgotten doses are principal reported causes of poor adherence; age and educational level have also been associated with it. Reminder approaches can be tailored to the patient, Grade C, and include alarms, internet tools, SMS messages, social networks, apps, and monitoring systems. Education and effective clinician–patient communication are important, Grade C. 1 randomized study suggested that follow-up every 3 months improves adherence compared with visits every 6 or 12 months, Grade B. Table 6 recommends explaining the need for regular dosing and completion of treatment, using reminders, and considering follow-up every 3 mo for SLIT.

document_sections.heading: 7 | HOW LONG AIT SHOULD BE CONTINUED FOR IN AR?
document_sections.content: Most AIT efficacy studies followed participants for 1 or 2 years during treatment. EMA recommends a randomized controlled study design with 3 years of treatment and 2 years of follow-up after cessation. Studies of grass-pollen SLIT tablets found benefit persisting for 2 years after 3 years of treatment. For HDM, 1 RCT suggested benefit lasting at least 1 year after 1 year of SLIT tablet treatment; a SLIT-drop RCT suggested persistence after 3 years of treatment. More HDM evidence, including the optimal duration, is needed. Grass-pollen SCIT given for 3-4 years produced benefit persisting for 3 years after discontinuation. In another study, SCIT and SLIT tablets outperformed placebo during 2 years of treatment, but 2 years did not produce long-term efficacy when assessed 1 year after cessation. An adult ragweed study reported continued benefit 2 years after 3 years of SCIT. Children assigned to 3 or 5 years of HDM SCIT had similar outcomes at 5 years. AIT can yield benefit from its first year, as summarized in Table 7. For lasting efficacy after cessation in AR, at least 3 years of AIT is recommended, Grade A.

document_sections.heading: 8 | ADVERSE EVENTS WITH AIT FOR AR
document_sections.content: Table 8 presents graded safety recommendations for appropriately selected patients receiving SCIT or SLIT, including asthma control, antihistamine premedication, observation, trained personnel, response to severe reactions, and patient education. Severe reactions require reassessment of treatment benefits and risks, with decisions and dosing changes aligned with the SmPC.

document_sections.heading: 8.1 | SCIT
document_sections.content: SCIT is generally safe and well tolerated when experienced staff administer injections in a medical setting, recognize systemic reactions early, and can manage them. Resuscitation equipment and a physician trained in anaphylaxis management must be immediately available, Grade C. Systemic reactions can involve skin, airways, gastrointestinal tract, or cardiovascular system and range from mild to severe. A 3year US routine-care survey covering over 20 million injection visits reported systemic reactions with 0.1% of injections and no deaths; a later survey by the same group reported 4 deaths, and earlier surveys also reported fatal reactions. Over 80% occurred within 30 minutes of injection, and very few later reactions were severe. Observation in the clinic for at least 30 minutes after each injection is recommended, Grade C. A European prospective survey of 4316 patients found systemic reactions in 2.1% of SCIT-treated patients. Its independent risk factors included natural extracts, absence of symptomatic allergy medication, asthma, animal-dander or pollen sensitization, cluster rather than rush regimens, and previous anaphylaxis. Other listed potential risk factors include current allergy symptoms or exposure, infection, mast cell disease, previous systemic AIT reaction, uncontrolled or severe asthma, high sensitization, excessive dose escalation, beta-blockers, poor injection technique, overdose, failure to reduce doses when changing batches, and high-intensity exercise. After 1 or more severe reactions, an allergist should reassess benefits and risks with the patient and decide whether SCIT should continue, Grade D; stopping or adjusting subsequent doses should follow the SmPC. Injection-site redness, itching, or swelling occurs after around half of injections. Cooling, topical glucocorticoids, or oral antihistamines may help. More local reactions do not predict a higher individual systemic-reaction risk. For injection-site redness or swelling >10 cm in diameter, subsequent-dose adjustment is described in the SmPC. H1-antihistamine premedication can reduce the frequency and severity of local reactions, Grade A, but cannot prevent systemic reactions or anaphylaxis. Modified extracts have been associated with fewer adverse effects in cited studies. Aluminum hydroxide-containing SCIT has been associated with granulomas, principally after incorrect intradermal administration, and with contact allergy, new protein contact dermatitis, or inflammatory vasculitis reactions. If these occur, a product without aluminum hydroxide is preferred, Grade D.

document_sections.heading: 8.2 | SLIT
document_sections.content: SLIT is generally safe and well tolerated. Severe systemic reactions appear substantially less likely than with SCIT, although overall adverse-event rates are similar. A review of 66 studies, including over 4000 SLIT recipients and over a million doses, found approximately 1 systemic reaction per 4 years of treatment and 1 severe systemic reaction per 384 treatment years. More recent studies raised no new safety concern. Severe reactions, sometimes including anaphylaxis, have occurred within 30 minutes after tablets or drops, in reported cases involving departures from usual standards such as nonstandardized extracts, rush schedules, excessive dosing, or prior discontinuation of SCIT after severe reactions. The first SLIT dose should be given under staff supervision capable of managing anaphylaxis, Grade C, with observation for at least 30 minutes, Grade C. Uncontrolled coexisting asthma has been reported with severe SLIT systemic reactions. A European survey found systemic reactions in 1.1% of SLIT-treated patients. Because most SLIT adverse events develop at home, patients should be taught to identify and manage them, especially severe reactions, and to respond to missed doses or situations requiring temporary interruption, Grade D. After 1 or more severe reactions, an allergist should revisit benefits and risks with the patient and decide whether to continue, Grade D; dose adjustment or cessation should follow the SmPC. Local SLIT adverse events correlate with dose and were reported in 40-75%, including transient oral pruritus or dysesthesia, oral swelling, throat irritation, and abdominal pain. They occur mainly early in treatment, commonly during the first 3 weeks, and are usually mild and self-limited. They nevertheless led to discontinuation in 4-8% of cases in recent tablet trials. Oral antihistamines may reduce local reactions, Grade A. Temporary interruption may be advised for 7 days after dental extraction, oral surgery, or loss of a deciduous tooth; while an oral ulcer or wound heals; or during an upper respiratory infection in a patient with asthma. Product SmPCs may provide further instructions.

document_sections.heading: 9 | PREVENTIVE EFFECTS OF AIT FOR AR
document_sections.content: Evidence cited by the guideline indicates that 3 years of AIT lowers the likelihood of asthma developing in children and adolescents whose allergic rhinitis is driven by pollen, with an effect lasting up to 2 years post-AIT. There is currently no convincing evidence that HDM AIT prevents asthma or that AIT prevents new sensitizations.

document_sections.heading: 10 | PHARMACOECONOMIC ASPECTS OF AIT VERSUS PHARMACOTHERAPY FOR AR
document_sections.content: Studies assessing monetary costs alone report favorable long-run healthcare spending with AIT, but do not expect savings in the first year. Most pharmacoeconomic studies support value for money, with cost-effectiveness within 6 years of starting treatment. Observational studies found pharmacotherapy-spending reductions of 12% to 80% with SCIT or SLIT. Several comparisons reported lower medical costs for AIT than placebo, but those savings did not cover AIT's own cost. Cost-effectiveness and cost-utility analyses additionally assess clinical benefit or quality-adjusted life years (QALYs); an ICER expresses cost relative to benefit. Several studies found SCIT and SLIT economically favorable compared with medication. 7 RCT-based studies from a health-system perspective suggested that either route would meet the United Kingdom NICE threshold of £20 000 (€24 616) per QALY for this population. Direct economic comparisons between SCIT and SLIT produced mixed results, so neither can be identified as more cost-effective. ICERs vary markedly between health systems, limiting generalization across countries. Study quality, incomplete characterization of uncertainty, and handling of missing data limit interpretation.

document_sections.heading: 11 | SUMMARY, GAPS IN THE EVIDENCE AND FUTURE PERSPECTIVES
document_sections.content: This EAACI guideline provides systematic-review- and meta-analysis-informed recommendations for AIT in AR, with or without conjunctivitis. Figure 2 compares SCIT and SLIT to support individual choice: it weighs seasonal and perennial efficacy, long-term evidence, injections versus home dosing, observation, adherence, adverse effects, costs, clinic visits, product availability, and patient preference. Figure 3 follows care from self-treatment through primary-care optimization and specialist assessment to supervised AIT, repeated reassessment, and cessation. Its cessation considerations include unacceptable adverse events, reassessment when patient and physician perceive no benefit after 1 y, and treatment for at least 3 y, with longer courses potentially appropriate for selected patients. Practical guidance calls for diagnostic and anaphylaxis-management expertise, appropriate facilities, documented product efficacy, assessment of contraindications, communication with patients, and follow-up for adherence and adverse effects. Table 9 addresses implementation barriers, facilitators, audit measures, and resources. The guideline's principal limitation is substantial heterogeneity in parts of its meta-analysis. Newer grass-pollen and HDM SLIT tablets have consistent low-risk-of-bias evidence, whereas older products, including HDM SCIT, have weaker support because trials differed and were often poorly designed or reported. Some older reports do not make clear whether analyses were intention-to-treat or per-protocol, preventing like-for-like pooling. Indirect comparisons suggest that products differ in efficacy; network analysis might improve comparative estimates, but varying European regulations and product availability complicate continent-wide product-specific recommendations. Before prescribing, clinicians should assess evidence for the individual product, emphasizing low-risk-of-bias studies. Important gaps include low-risk-of-bias pediatric trials, evidence after treatment cessation—especially for HDM—research in older adults with multimorbidity, dose-finding work, agreement on a clinically meaningful effect size, patient-reported outcomes, randomized economic studies, predictive biomarkers, and improved adherence. Consistent international terminology and grading, including MedDRA and WAO classifications, would improve adverse-event comparisons. Table 10 prioritizes these and further gaps, including allergen mixtures, contraindications, provocation tests, pregnancy management, orphan extracts, and approaches to reducing adverse effects. Large controlled routine-care datasets may supplement randomized prospective evidence, provided bias and confounding are acknowledged. Despite these limitations, evidence supports SCIT, SLIT tablets, and SLIT drops for adults and children with moderate-to-severe AR inadequately controlled by medication. Wider access will require awareness among primary-care professionals, healthcare providers, patients, and support groups, alongside implementation materials and updates as evidence develops.
